title: Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. (1980)
summary: Rule 3 did not displace the state rule tying timely commencement for limitations purposes to service.
notes:
A federal and state provision can use related vocabulary without regulating exactly the same legal consequence. Identify the precise question: commencing federal procedure, serving process, or preserving a claim against limitations.

Walker, an Oklahoma carpenter injured by a defective nail on August 22, 1975, filed in federal court on August 19, 1977 (three days before the two-year limit) but did not serve Armco until December 1, 1977, outside Oklahoma's 60-day service window; the district court dismissed, the Tenth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding Rule 3 was not sufficiently broad to control the issue and was not intended to toll state limitations periods.

sections.Parties: Walker brought a product-related injury claim against Armco Steel.
sections.Material Facts: The complaint was filed within the state limitations period, but the defendant was served after the period and the additional service interval permitted by state law. The plaintiff argued that filing under Rule 3 commenced the federal action and therefore satisfied the limitations requirement.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court applied the state limitations rule and reaffirmed the relevant interpretation of Ragan after Hanna.
sections.Issue: Did Federal Rule 3 answer the same limitations-tolling question as the state service rule and therefore displace it under Hanna?
sections.Holding: No. Rule 3 governed commencement of the federal action for procedural purposes, but did not supply the asserted state-limitations tolling rule.
sections.Reasoning: Before asking whether a Federal Rule is valid, the court must determine whether it actually governs the disputed point. Rule 3 could operate according to its terms while the state statute independently determined whether the state-created claim was time-barred. The state service requirement was integral to the limitations scheme, so ignoring it would give the federal plaintiff a different right to recover. This was not Hanna’s direct conflict between alternative permissible methods of service.

learning.why: Rule 3 did not displace the state rule tying timely commencement for limitations purposes to service.

topics.cp-rule-scope: Rule 3’s commencement provision did not purport to toll the state limitations period. Hanna’s Federal-Rule analysis applies only after identifying a genuinely governing federal rule.
topics.cp-limitations: The state service requirement was part of the operation of its limitations scheme.
topics.cp-erie: Walker is a core Erie case on the threshold question of whether a Federal Rule actually governs before Hanna's analysis applies.
topics.cp-erie-accommodation: The Court read Rule 3 narrowly so that it and the state service-based commencement rule could each control its own sphere without conflict.

mnemonic.rationale: A nail, and sixty days to serve
